notes.body: CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 is the current version of the exam. Its published format: up to 90 questions, 90 minutes, multiple-choice plus performance-based questions (PBQs), and a passing score of 750 on a 100-900 scale. The five domains and their weights are: 1.0 General Security Concepts at 12 percent, 2.0 Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations at 22 percent, 3.0 Security Architecture at 18 percent, 4.0 Security Operations at 28 percent, and 5.0 Security Program Management and Oversight at 20 percent. Add the weights: 12 + 22 + 18 + 28 + 20 = 100. That single arithmetic check tells you the blueprint is a zero-sum budget of your study time: Security Operations alone is worth more than domains 1 and 3 combined. Worked example — pacing math. Ninety minutes for up to 90 questions means a nominal pace of one question per minute. But PBQs (drag-and-drop network diagrams, firewall rule matching, log triage simulations) can consume five to eight minutes each, and there are typically a few of them. The working method: on your first pass, answer everything you can solve in under a minute, flag PBQs and any question needing more than ninety seconds, and finish the pass with about 55-60 minutes elapsed. Your second pass then owns the flagged set with the remaining time. Never leave a question unanswered — there is no penalty for a wrong answer, and a blank is a guaranteed zero. Common mistake: treating 750/900 as 83 percent and therefore deciding you need to master 83 percent of everything. The scale is not a raw percentage; it is a scaled score, and CompTIA does not publish the raw-to-scaled conversion. The practical takeaway is simpler: you need a comfortable majority of questions correct, and because questions are distributed roughly by domain weight, your heaviest domain (Security Operations, 28 percent) is also where the most points live. A second gotcha: people walk in having memorized definitions but having never practiced PBQ-style tasks. CompTIA's performance-based questions test whether you can DO the thing — match the log to the attack, order the incident-response steps, place the control in the architecture. Every lab in IL-29 is practice for that exact skill. Your exam-day checklist therefore has two halves: know the five domains cold (definitions and classifications), and be able to perform the operational tasks in domains 2 through 4 under time pressure. One more exam-day mechanic: CompTIA randomizes question order, so your first pass is really a hunt for quick wins across the whole exam. Practice this on every timed set - never answer sequentially out of habit. And remember that PBQs are often front-loaded; if the first screen is a simulation, breathe, flag it, and start with question two. The points are identical wherever they sit, and confidence compounds: banking ten quick wins in the first fifteen minutes changes how you handle the hard questions later.
notes.title: The SY0-701 exam blueprint: format, pacing, and question mix

notes.body: Domain 1.0 is the vocabulary layer every other domain assumes. Its core ideas: the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity, availability) and its extended family (authentication, non-repudiation); the AAA framework (authentication, authorization, accounting); zero trust principles (never trust, always verify; assume breach; verify explicitly; least privilege; microsegmentation); physical security controls; deception and disruption technology (honeypots, honeynets, honeytokens); and control types and categories. Control types are the exam's favorite classification game. Types: technical (implemented in systems — firewalls, encryption, MFA), managerial (policies, procedures, risk assessments), operational (human processes — guards, awareness training, background checks), and physical (locks, cameras, mantraps). Categories: preventive (stop the event — firewall rules, least privilege), detective (find the event — IDS, log monitoring, audits), corrective (fix after the event — backups, patches, incident response), compensating (alternative when the ideal control is infeasible — a camera where a guard cannot be posted), and directive (steer behavior — policies, signage). Worked example. Scenario: 'A company places a honeypot server on its network to attract and study attackers.' Classification: this is a deception technology, and as a control it is technical (a system) and detective (it reveals attacker activity), deployed at the network/host layer. Second scenario: 'An organization requires security awareness training for all new hires.' Classification: operational control, directive category — it shapes human behavior rather than blocking an attack directly. Common mistake: calling a honeypot a preventive control. It does not prevent the initial intrusion; it detects and studies it, so it is detective. Another classic: confusing compensating with corrective. A compensating control is a substitute adopted because the primary control cannot be implemented; a corrective control restores normal operations after an incident. Zero trust appears here as a concept and then haunts the entire exam: every question about network design, access control, or endpoint policy is secretly asking whether you applied never-trust-always-verify and least privilege. When you read any SY0-701 question, first ask which control type and category is in play — half the distractors die at that step. A third worked example ties it together. Scenario: 'A company stores backups offline in a fireproof safe and tests restores quarterly.' Classification: the offline backup is a corrective control (it restores operations after an incident), implemented technically and physically, and the quarterly test is a managerial detective control (it verifies the corrective control works). Exam stems often bundle two controls - classify each separately and you will not be fooled. Also drill the zero-trust vocabulary until it is boring: 'never trust, always verify' is the phrase the exam wants, and every scenario about implicit trust (VPN users treated as safe, internal traffic uninspected) is a zero-trust violation. When a question asks for the BEST long-term fix for lateral movement after a phishing breach, the zero-trust answer - microsegmentation plus least privilege - beats 'a bigger firewall' every time.
notes.title: Domain 1.0 — General Security Concepts (12%): the language of the whole exam

notes.body: This is the second-heaviest domain and the one most people find intuitive, because it is the attacker-and-weakness catalog. It covers threat actors (their motivations and resources — nation-state, hacktivist, insider threat, organized crime, shadow IT as an internal risk), attack vectors and attack surfaces, malware families (ransomware, trojans, worms, rootkits, keyloggers, spyware, logic bombs, RATs), social engineering (phishing, spear phishing, whaling, vishing, smishing, pretexting, baiting, watering-hole attacks), vulnerability types (zero-day, misconfigurations, weak defaults, unpatched software, buffer overflows, race conditions, memory injection), and mitigation techniques (patching, hardening, segmentation, encryption, least privilege, secure baselines). Worked example — threat classification. Scenario: 'An attacker calls the help desk claiming to be the CFO, urgently requesting a password reset for the finance share.' This is pretexting (a fabricated scenario to manipulate) delivered via vishing (voice phishing). The mitigation stack: verify identity through an independent channel (callback to a known number), enforce a password-reset workflow that does not rely on caller claims, and train help-desk staff on social engineering — which ties back to Domain 1's operational/directive controls. Second worked example — vulnerability triage. 'A public-facing web server runs a version with a known remote-code-execution flaw; the vendor released a patch yesterday; the server cannot go down during business hours.' The vulnerability is an unpatched known flaw (not a zero-day — a patch exists). Mitigation: schedule an emergency change window, and as an interim compensating control, put the server behind a WAF rule blocking the exploit pattern and restrict its network reachability (segmentation). Common mistakes: calling every phishing email 'spear phishing' — spear phishing is targeted at a specific person or role; a mass credential-harvest email is just phishing. Calling a trojan a virus — viruses self-replicate by attaching to host files, worms self-propagate across networks, trojans disguise themselves as legitimate software and do not self-replicate. On exam day, underline the propagation mechanism in the question stem; it is almost always the discriminator between malware answers. A third worked example - attack surface reasoning. Scenario: 'An attacker scans the public IP range, finds an exposed RDP port, and brute-forces a weak password.' The attack vector is the exposed RDP service (attack surface: internet-facing remote access); the vulnerability is the weak password plus the exposed service; the mitigation stack is layered - remove RDP from the internet (attack-surface reduction), enforce MFA and account lockout (credential hardening), and put the service behind a VPN or jump host (network control). Exam questions love asking for the BEST mitigation, and the best answer is usually the one that shrinks the attack surface rather than the one that polices it. Common trap: choosing 'install antivirus' for a network-exposure problem - the vector is the exposure, so the fix must address the exposure. Another: confusing a vulnerability (the weakness) with a threat (the actor or event that exploits it). The weak password is the vulnerability; the brute-forcing attacker is the threat; together they create risk. Keep those three nouns straight and Domain 2.0 scenario stems become classification exercises.
notes.title: Domain 2.0 — Threats, Vulnerabilities, and Mitigations (22%)

notes.body: Domain 3.0 asks how secure systems are built: cloud models and the shared responsibility model, virtualization and containerization security, network architecture (segmentation, DMZ, VLANs, VPNs, SD-WAN), resilience and recovery (redundancy, backups, high availability, disaster recovery vs. business continuity), and secure protocols. The shared responsibility model is the single most-tested idea here. In IaaS the provider secures the physical infrastructure, virtualization layer, and network fabric; you secure the OS, applications, data, and access. In PaaS the provider additionally owns the OS and runtime; you own the application code, data, and identity. In SaaS the provider owns nearly everything up to the application; you own your data, user access, and configuration. Worked example. Scenario: 'A company migrates its customer database to a SaaS CRM. A misconfigured sharing setting exposes customer records to the internet.' Who failed? The customer. Under shared responsibility, the SaaS provider secures the platform; the tenant owns its data and its access configuration. The fix is a configuration review and a data-classification policy, not a ticket to the vendor. Second worked example — architecture choice. 'An industrial control network must never route traffic to the corporate LAN, but engineers need occasional remote diagnostics.' The design answer is segmentation with a jump host (a hardened, monitored bastion in a DMZ-like boundary zone), plus VPN with MFA for the remote leg — defense in depth with the smallest possible trust bridge. Common mistakes: recommending a VPN as if it were segmentation — a VPN extends a network, it does not divide one; and confusing disaster recovery (restoring IT systems, measured by RTO/RPO) with business continuity (keeping the business functioning during disruption). Also know your protocols cold: DNS on 53, HTTP 80, HTTPS 443, SSH 22, RDP 3389, SMB 445, LDAP 389/636, SMTP 25/587, SNMP 161, FTP 20/21, TFTP 69, DHCP 67/68, NTP 123, IMAP 143/993, POP3 110/995, Telnet 23 (and why you never use it). Protocol-and-port matching is easy points if you drill it and easy losses if you do not. A third worked example - resilience math in plain language. 'The business needs the ordering system back within 4 hours of a failure, and can afford to lose at most 1 hour of transactions.' That is an RTO of 4 hours (recovery time objective: how fast) and an RPO of 1 hour (recovery point objective: how much data loss). The architecture answer: backups at least hourly (to meet the RPO) plus a tested restore procedure that completes inside 4 hours (to meet the RTO). Exam stems give you the business requirement and ask which backup strategy fits - match the frequency to the RPO and the restore speed to the RTO. Common mistake: swapping the two. RTO is about time to recover; RPO is about data loss tolerance. A second gotcha: high availability (keeping the system running through failures - clustering, redundancy) vs. fault tolerance (continuing through a component failure with zero interruption). Both serve availability, but fault tolerance is the stronger guarantee.
notes.title: Domain 3.0 — Security Architecture (18%): designing it right

notes.body: At 28 percent, Security Operations is the largest slice of the exam and the most operational — this is where your IL-29 hands-on depth pays off. It covers SOC operations and SIEM (log aggregation, correlation rules, alert triage, tuning to kill false positives), vulnerability management (scanning, prioritization, remediation workflows), incident response (the lifecycle: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned), digital forensics basics (order of volatility, chain of custody, imaging), and the security tools of the trade: IDS/IPS, EDR, DLP, firewalls, honeypots, vulnerability scanners, penetration testing vs. vulnerability assessment. Worked example — SIEM triage. You are shown three alerts: (1) a single failed SSH login from an internal workstation, (2) 400 failed SSH logins in 10 minutes from one external IP against a public server, (3) a successful login immediately following alert 2 from the same IP. Analysis: alert 1 is noise (single failure, internal source — likely a typo). Alert 2 is a brute-force/password-spray pattern — a detective control firing as designed. Alert 3 is the critical one: successful authentication after a brute-force burst means probable compromise; the correct action is to contain first (isolate the host, disable the account, rotate credentials), then investigate. This is the exam's favorite ladder: noise, then attack pattern, then successful compromise — and the right answer is always the one that matches the incident-response phase you are in. Second worked example — vulnerability prioritization. A scanner reports: a critical RCE on an internet-facing server, a high-severity flaw on an isolated test VM, and a medium flaw on a domain controller. Priority order: internet-facing critical RCE first (exploitability times exposure), then the domain controller medium (asset criticality elevates it), then the isolated test VM last. Common mistakes: confusing IDS (detective, alerts only) with IPS (preventive, blocks inline); confusing a vulnerability scan (finds weaknesses, no exploitation) with a penetration test (authorized simulated attack, exploits within scope); and answering forensics questions without respecting the order of volatility — registers and cache first, then RAM, then disk, then logs — because volatile evidence dies when you power down. A third worked example - the EDR vs. antivirus question the exam loves. 'A fileless attack runs entirely in memory via PowerShell.' Traditional signature antivirus sees no file and stays silent; EDR sees the process behavior - PowerShell spawning from Word, obfuscated commands, C2 beaconing - and kills the chain. The exam discriminator: signature-based tools match known files; behavior-based tools (EDR) match malicious actions. When the stem says 'fileless,' 'living off the land,' or 'zero-day,' the answer is the behavioral tool. Common mistake: treating DLP as a network-only control - DLP spans endpoint, network, and cloud, watching data in use, in motion, and at rest. And a final Domain 4.0 trap: penetration testing requires written authorization defining scope - the exam treats an unauthorized 'helpful' test as an attack, and the correct answer always starts with the rules of engagement.
notes.title: Domain 4.0 — Security Operations (28%): the heaviest domain, where points live

notes.body: Domain 5.0 is the governance domain: risk management, policies and frameworks, compliance, audits, privacy, and third-party risk. The exam tests whether you think like someone running a security program, not just operating its tools. Risk management vocabulary is the core: a threat is what could happen, a vulnerability is the weakness it exploits, risk is the combination (commonly expressed as likelihood times impact), a risk assessment identifies and evaluates risks, and risk responses are avoid, transfer (insurance, outsourcing), mitigate (apply controls), or accept (document the residual risk and move on). Worked example — risk math. A ransomware attack on the file server is estimated at 30 percent annual likelihood with a $200,000 impact. Annualized risk: 0.30 x 200,000 = $60,000. A backup-and-recovery control costs $25,000 per year and cuts likelihood to 5 percent: new risk = 0.05 x 200,000 = $10,000, plus the $25,000 control cost = $35,000 total, which is less than the $60,000 exposure — so the control is cost-justified. That is the entire logic of risk-based decision making in one calculation, and exam questions dress it in scenarios about whether to buy the control, buy insurance (transfer), or accept. Frameworks and compliance: know what the big names govern without memorizing their clause numbers. NIST CSF organizes cybersecurity outcomes; NIST RMF structures federal risk management; ISO 27001/27002 cover information security management; PCI DSS governs cardholder data; HIPAA governs protected health information; GDPR governs EU personal data; SOC 2 reports on service-organization controls. Privacy concepts: data classification (public, internal, confidential, restricted), data retention and disposal, and the principle of collecting the minimum data necessary. Third-party risk: vendor assessments, right-to-audit clauses, and supply-chain risk — you inherit the security posture of everyone you connect to. Common mistake: answering governance questions with a technical control. When the question asks what the CISO should do about a policy gap, the answer is a governance action (update the policy, run a risk assessment, commission an audit), not 'install a firewall.' A second worked example - the policy hierarchy. 'An employee violates the acceptable-use policy by mining crypto on a workstation.' The policy (managerial, directive) defined the rule; the monitoring that caught it was detective; the disciplinary process is the enforcement. Exam questions ask which document governs a situation - policies set direction, standards set the mandatory rules, procedures give step-by-step instructions, guidelines are recommendations. The discriminator: 'must' language lives in standards, 'how to' lives in procedures. A third mini-example: third-party risk. 'The company adopts a SaaS vendor that suffers a breach.' The controls that should have existed: a vendor risk assessment before signing, a right-to-audit clause in the contract, and a review of the vendor's SOC 2 report. On the exam, supply-chain and vendor questions are always answered with assessment-before-trust - never 'the vendor handles it.'
notes.title: Domain 5.0 — Security Program Management and Oversight (20%)

notes.body: Here is how this course maps to the five domains, so you can study with a plan instead of a pile. Domain 1.0 (General Security Concepts, 12%): lean on IL-29's zero-trust foundations, control-type drills, and crypto/prereq-math modules — the vocabulary is already in your notes. Domain 2.0 (Threats/Vulnerabilities/Mitigations, 22%): use the threat-modeling, malware-analysis, and MITRE ATT&CK modules; build a personal malware-family flashcard set until you can name the propagation mechanism of each family in under five seconds. Domain 3.0 (Security Architecture, 18%): use the network-security, cloud-security, and secure-architecture modules; drill protocol-port pairs and the shared responsibility model until both are reflex. Domain 4.0 (Security Operations, 28%): this is your heaviest investment — the SIEM/log-analysis, vulnerability-management, incident-response, and forensics modules, plus every hands-on lab, because this domain tests doing, not reciting. Domain 5.0 (Program Management, 20%): use the governance/risk/compliance modules; practice risk calculations and framework-matching until the vocabulary is boring. Worked example — a four-week schedule. Week 1: domains 1 and 5 (concepts + governance, lighter reading, build your flashcard decks). Week 2: domain 2 (threats — heavy memorization, daily 20-minute malware/social-engineering drills). Week 3: domain 3 (architecture — whiteboard network designs, protocol-port drills). Week 4: domain 4 (operations — full labs, timed log-triage sets, incident-response ordering drills). Every week ends with a mixed 30-question set; the final three days are full timed runs. The timed practice gate is your go/no-go decision. Build a 90-question mixed set (or two 45-question halves), enforce 90 minutes with no pauses, score it, and break the score down by domain. Gate rule: overall scaled-equivalent at least 80 percent correct AND no domain below 65 percent correct. If Security Operations is at 58 percent, you do not schedule the exam — you do another week of domain 4 labs. Operator gotcha: most people fail practice gates on pacing, not knowledge — they spend six minutes on one PBQ-style scenario and then rush twenty questions. Practice the flag-and-return discipline from note 1 on every timed run until it is automatic. Schedule the real exam only after two consecutive gate passes on fresh question sets. One more planning tool: the error log. After every practice set, record each miss in four buckets - knowledge gap (never learned it), misread stem (knew it, rushed it), pacing casualty (ran out of time), distractor trap (fell for the tempting wrong answer). After three sets, the buckets reveal your real enemy: knowledge gaps need study blocks, misreads need slower first-pass discipline, pacing casualties need stricter flag-and-return, distractor traps need the 'what is the question REALLY asking' habit. Most candidates discover their enemy is not knowledge but process - and process is fixable in days, not weeks. Review the log before each new set; watching the same trap catch you twice is the only unforgivable error in this plan.

Build two more fresh sets (timed-set-2.md, timed-set-3.md) — never reuse questions.
Repeat until all three sets score 80%+ with documented tuning history.
Write a final paragraph in triage-log.md: which rule-tuning lesson was most important and why.

notes.body: CompTIA CySA+ CS0-003 is the current version of the exam. Its published format: a maximum of 85 questions, multiple-choice plus performance-based questions, 165 minutes, passing score 750/900. The four domains: 1.0 Security Operations at 33 percent, 2.0 Vulnerability Management at 30 percent, 3.0 Incident Response Management at 20 percent, and 4.0 Reporting and Communication at 17 percent. Check the arithmetic: 33 + 30 + 20 + 17 = 100. Notice the shape of this exam compared with Security+: CySA+ is almost two-thirds operations and vulnerability work (63 percent combined). It assumes you already know the Security+ vocabulary and tests whether you can do analyst work — read logs, prioritize findings, run an incident, and write the report. Worked example — pacing. One hundred sixty-five minutes over a maximum of 85 questions is roughly two minutes per question, more generous than Security+. But the performance-based questions here are heavier: analyzing a log bundle, tuning a correlation rule, ordering an incident-response workflow, or building a vulnerability-prioritization matrix can take eight to twelve minutes each. Apply the same flag-and-return discipline: first pass for everything answerable in under two minutes, second pass for the flagged PBQs, never leave blanks. A common mistake is treating CySA+ as 'Security+ part 2' and studying more definitions. The definitions are prerequisites; the exam tests judgment. When you read a stem, ask: what would an analyst do next in the SOC? The answer choices that describe analyst actions (tune the rule, isolate the host, prioritize by exploitability) beat the ones that describe memorized facts. Second gotcha: performance-based questions often have multiple defensible answers but one best action — the exam rewards the action that matches the phase of work you are in. If you are in detection, you investigate; if you are in containment, you isolate; if the incident is over, you write the lessons learned. Matching your action to the phase is the master key to Domain 3.0 questions. A second pacing scenario, because CySA+ PBQs are the real time sink. Suppose the exam serves you 80 multiple-choice and 5 PBQs. At two minutes each, the multiple-choice costs 160 minutes - already over budget. That arithmetic is why flag-and-return is non-negotiable: answer the 60 multiple-choice you know in about 70 minutes, bank them, then spend the remaining 95 minutes on the 20 harder multiple-choice plus the 5 PBQs. The candidates who fail CySA+ on time usually did the opposite - they wrestled each PBQ in order and never reached the last 25 questions. Also note the psychological shape: CySA+ stems are longer than Security+'s, with log snippets and scenario setups. Train yourself to read the actual question FIRST (the last sentence), then read the stem for exactly what it asks. Analysts who read the whole log bundle before knowing the question burn ten minutes on data they never needed - the same discipline as a real SOC queue, and the exam is deliberately testing it.
notes.title: The CS0-003 blueprint: analyst work under a 165-minute clock

notes.body: At 33 percent, Security Operations is the heart of CySA+. It covers SOC workflow, SIEM engineering (log sources, correlation rules, alert tuning), threat hunting (hypothesis-driven searching for undetected threats), detection types and the confusion matrix of detection (true positive, false positive, true negative, false negative), and continuous monitoring. Worked example — the detection matrix. A SIEM rule watches for impossible-travel logins. Case A: an attacker logs in from two countries minutes apart and the rule fires — true positive (real attack, alert fired). Case B: an employee uses a VPN endpoint in another country and the rule fires — false positive (no attack, alert fired). Case C: an attacker uses a residential proxy in the same city and the rule stays silent — false negative (real attack, no alert). Case D: normal logins, no alert — true negative. The false negative is the dangerous one; the false positive is the expensive one (analyst time). Tuning a rule is the eternal trade: tighten it and false positives drop but false negatives rise; loosen it and you catch more at the cost of noise. Second worked example — threat hunting. An intel report describes a new ransomware group using scheduled tasks named like system utilities. No alerts have fired. The analyst hypothesizes the group may already be present, queries EDR data for scheduled-task creations with mismatched names, and finds three. That is threat hunting: you start from a hypothesis and go looking instead of waiting for alerts. Common mistakes: confusing threat hunting (proactive, hypothesis-driven) with alert triage (reactive, queue-driven); and answering SIEM questions with 'buy more log sources' when the scenario shows the data already exists — the analyst's job is usually correlation and tuning, not procurement. Also: continuous monitoring is not a tool, it is the practice — the SOC never stops watching, and the exam treats monitoring gaps as findings. A third worked example - alert tuning as an exam scenario. 'A correlation rule fires 300 times daily on legitimate vulnerability-scanner traffic, and analysts now ignore the rule entirely.' The diagnosis: a false-positive flood causing alert fatigue - which is operationally equivalent to a false negative, because real attacks hide in the ignored noise. The fix: tune the rule to exclude the scanner's IP range or require a second indicator (e.g., scanner traffic PLUS an unexpected process launch), then verify the tuned rule still fires on a known-bad test case. The exam tests this as a process question: the wrong answers are 'disable the rule' (creates a real blind spot) and 'hire more analysts' (scales the noise). The right answer is always tuning with verification. Common mistake: confusing continuous monitoring with a tool purchase. Monitoring is the practice - log sources feeding correlation feeding triage, around the clock. The exam treats 'we bought a SIEM but nobody watches the queue on weekends' as a monitoring failure, and the finding is process, not product.
notes.title: Domain 1.0 — Security Operations (33%): the SOC analyst's domain

notes.body: At 30 percent, Vulnerability Management is the second pillar: find weaknesses, prioritize them, remediate or compensate, and verify. It covers scanning (credentialed vs. non-credentialed, agent-based vs. network-based), vulnerability classification and scoring concepts, prioritization, remediation workflows, and compensating controls when patching is infeasible. Worked example — prioritization. Three findings: (A) a critical remote-code-execution flaw with a public exploit, on the internet-facing web server; (B) a critical flaw with no public exploit, on an isolated test VM; (C) a medium flaw on the domain controller. The exam's prioritization formula is exploitability x exposure x asset criticality. A wins outright: weaponized, exposed, production. Between B and C: C — the domain controller's criticality elevates a medium flaw above an isolated theoretical critical. So the order is A, C, B. Memorize that logic; it answers half the Domain 2.0 scenario questions. Second worked example — the remediation workflow. A scan finds an unpatched service on 40 workstations. The analyst validates the finding (no false positive), prioritizes (widespread, exploitable, medium asset value), opens a change ticket, coordinates a maintenance window, deploys the patch to a pilot group, verifies, rolls out fully, then rescans to confirm closure. Skipping the rescan is the classic operational failure — unverified remediation is an open finding. Common mistakes: treating a vulnerability scan as a penetration test (scanning finds weaknesses without exploiting; pen testing is an authorized attack that exploits within scope); calling every unpatched system a 'zero-day' (zero-day means no patch exists — if a patch exists and was not applied, it is an unpatched known vulnerability, and the fix is process, not research); and forgetting compensating controls — when the vendor patch is 30 days out, segmentation, WAF rules, and disabling the service are the correct interim answers, not 'wait for the patch.' A third worked example - the scan-types discriminator the exam loves. 'The team needs a complete inventory of missing patches on 500 workstations, including registry-level detail.' The answer is a credentialed scan: with valid credentials, the scanner reads the registry and patch history directly - accurate and fast. A non-credentialed scan would only infer from network banners, missing half the findings. Contrast: 'The team wants to see what an external attacker sees.' That is a non-credentialed, external scan - no credentials, attacker's view. The exam pairs these deliberately; match the scan type to the goal. A second trap: scan timing. Credentialed scans during business hours can disrupt operations - the analyst's job includes scheduling, change control, and stakeholder notice, which is why vulnerability management is a program, not a button. And remember the lifecycle loop: scan, validate (kill false positives before you alarm anyone), prioritize (exploitability x exposure x criticality), remediate (change-controlled), rescan (verify closure). The exam's favorite wrong answer is any option that skips validation or the rescan - unverified findings waste everyone's time, and unverified fixes are open findings.
notes.title: Domain 2.0 — Vulnerability Management (30%): find, rank, fix, verify

notes.body: At 20 percent, Incident Response Management tests whether you can run an incident, not just describe one. The lifecycle: preparation (playbooks, tools, roles, tabletop exercises), detection and analysis (triage, scoping, confirming the incident), containment (short-term: isolate; long-term: cut off the attacker's access paths), eradication (remove the foothold, close the exploited vector), recovery (restore systems, monitor for re-infection), and lessons learned (post-incident review, playbook updates). Evidence handling runs alongside: maintain chain of custody, image before you analyze, respect the order of volatility. Worked example — a phishing-to-ransomware chain. Monday: a user clicks a link; EDR quarantines a payload (detection and analysis begins — is this an incident or an event?). Tuesday: the payload detonated before quarantine on one host and is moving laterally (confirmed incident — now containment: isolate the host, block the C2 domains at the firewall, disable the compromised account). Wednesday: the team removes persistence mechanisms and patches the exploited vector (eradication), then restores encrypted shares from immutable backups (recovery), then holds the post-incident review that discovers the phishing filter rule was disabled — and re-enables it with change control (lessons learned). Notice the discipline: you never eradicate before you contain (the attacker re-enters), and you never skip lessons learned (the same incident recurs). Second worked example — scoping. Three hosts show indicators; the analyst images all three before analysis begins, documents who handled each image and when (chain of custody), and only then starts the deep dive. Common mistakes: jumping to eradication ('just reimage it') before containment and scoping — you lose the evidence and the attacker's other footholds; confusing short-term containment (isolate the host now) with long-term containment (block the C2 infrastructure, rotate credentials enterprise-wide); and forgetting that preparation is a phase too — the team that runs tabletop exercises responds in minutes, the team that does not responds in days. A third worked example - the tabletop as preparation. 'The team runs a tabletop exercise: a simulated ransomware outbreak on a Friday afternoon.' The facilitator walks through each phase: who declares the incident, who isolates, who talks to legal, who decides on restoration. The value is not the scenario - it is discovering that nobody knows who can authorize isolating the finance VLAN. That discovery IS the exercise's product, and the playbook gets updated before a real incident tests it. The exam treats tabletops as a preparation-phase control and loves asking what a tabletop produces (findings about the plan, not about the attacker). Common mistake: confusing incident response with disaster recovery. IR handles the security event (stop the attacker, eradicate, recover securely); DR handles the restoration of IT services after any disruption (the RTO/RPO plan). They overlap at recovery but start from different triggers - the exam separates them by asking what initiated the response. A security incident triggers IR; a hurricane triggers DR and business continuity. Know which plan owns which trigger.
notes.title: Domain 3.0 — Incident Response Management (20%): run the incident

notes.body: At 17 percent, Reporting and Communication is the smallest domain but the one that separates analysts who get promoted from analysts who stay in the queue. It covers report types and audiences, metrics that matter, and stakeholder communication during incidents. The master rule: the report serves the audience, not the author. An executive report leads with business impact, risk, cost, and recommended actions in plain language — no packet dumps, no CVE strings without translation. A technical report gives engineers the indicators, timelines, affected systems, and remediation steps with enough detail to act. A compliance or legal report adds the notification timeline and the evidence-preservation record. Worked example. The same ransomware incident produces three documents. Executive summary (one page): 'On Tuesday, ransomware encrypted the finance share; operations were restored from backups within 8 hours; no customer data left the network; we recommend a $40,000 EDR upgrade and mandatory phishing training; residual risk is medium until the email-filter gap is closed.' Technical report: the full timeline, IOCs, the disabled filter rule, the containment actions with timestamps, the eradication steps, and the verification rescan results. Compliance memo: when the incident was declared, who was notified and when, what data was affected, and the chain-of-custody log for the forensic images. Common mistakes: writing the executive report like a technical one (executives do not care about the malware's mutex name; they care about impact and decisions); omitting recommended actions (a report that describes without recommending is a diary, not an analysis); and forgetting metrics — mean time to detect, mean time to respond, and vulnerability-remediation SLAs are the numbers that prove the security program works. In PBQs, the question often asks which document or which section goes to whom — answer with the audience rule and you will rarely miss. A second worked example - metrics that matter. 'The CISO asks whether the SOC is improving.' The analyst answers with three numbers: mean time to detect (MTTD) dropped from 4 hours to 45 minutes after the new correlation rules; mean time to respond (MTTR) dropped from 8 hours to 2 hours after the playbook update; and vulnerability-remediation SLA compliance rose from 60% to 92%. Those three metrics - MTTD, MTTR, SLA compliance - are the exam's favorite proof-of-program numbers, and any answer choice offering vanity metrics ('alerts processed,' 'logs collected') loses to them. A third mini-example: the compliance report. 'Regulators require evidence that access reviews happen quarterly.' The report includes the review dates, the reviewers, the findings, and the remediation - the who, when, what, and so-what. The exam tests whether you know that compliance reporting is evidence of process, not narrative. Common mistake: writing metrics without baselines. 'MTTR is 2 hours' means nothing; 'MTTR fell from 8 hours to 2 hours after the playbook update' proves improvement. Always pair the number with its before.
notes.title: Domain 4.0 — Reporting and Communication (17%): write for the reader

notes.body: IL-29 is built for exactly this exam's shape, so the mapping is direct. Domain 1.0 (Security Operations, 33%): use the SIEM, log-analysis, detection-engineering, and threat-hunting modules — plus every drill that asks you to read a log and name the attack. Your daily practice should be 20 minutes of log-triage sets; pattern recognition is a muscle. Domain 2.0 (Vulnerability Management, 30%): use the vulnerability-scanning, prioritization, and patch-management modules; run the prioritization formula (exploitability x exposure x asset criticality) on every scenario until it is reflex. Domain 3.0 (Incident Response Management, 20%): use the incident-response lifecycle modules and tabletop-style scenario drills; practice ordering the six phases and naming the correct action for the phase you are in. Domain 4.0 (Reporting and Communication, 17%): use the security-writing and governance modules; practice rewriting one technical finding per day into a three-sentence executive summary. Worked example — a five-week plan. Weeks 1-2: domains 1 and 2 (the 63 percent core — log sets daily, prioritization drills daily). Week 3: domain 3 (incident scenarios, tabletop walkthroughs, evidence-handling drills). Week 4: domain 4 plus your weakest domain from practice scores (report-writing reps, metrics flashcards). Week 5: full timed sets only. The CySA+ practice gate: build 85-question-equivalent sets (or scaled 40-question halves), enforce the proportional time (roughly 2 minutes per question), and score by domain. Gate rule: overall 80 percent or better AND no domain below 70 percent. CySA+ punishes shallow breadth — because the questions are scenario-heavy, a domain at 60 percent means you cannot do the analyst work yet, not that you forgot a definition. Operator gotcha: on PBQs that present a log bundle, read the question stem FIRST, then hunt the logs for exactly what the stem asks. Analysts who read all the logs before reading the question burn ten minutes on data they never needed — the same discipline you will use in a real SOC queue. A second worked example - the weekly rhythm in practice. Monday's 20-minute log set surfaces a weakness: you keep misclassifying beaconing as normal traffic. Tuesday through Thursday, every triage set includes two beaconing scenarios until the pattern is reflex. Friday's assessment: a fresh 15-question set where beaconing appears three times - you nail all three, and the crosswalk table gets a 'validated' mark for the detection topic. That is the plan working as designed: the scorecard finds the weakness, the reps fix it, the assessment proves it. A common failure mode is studying without the Friday assessment - reps without measurement drift into comfortable repetition of what you already know. The assessment is the forcing function; never skip it. And a final gate nuance: when you pass twice consecutively, change nothing about your routine for the last week before the exam except tapering volume. Athletes taper; analysts should too - the goal on exam day is sharp recall, not exhausted cramming.

notes.body: The CISSP (Certified Information Systems Security Professional), administered by ISC2, is the current 2024 eight-domain version. Its published format: 100 to 150 computer-adaptive (CAT) questions, 3 hours, passing score 700 out of 1000. The eight domains and their 2024 weights: 1. Security and Risk Management, 16 percent; 2. Asset Security, 10 percent; 3. Security Architecture and Engineering, 13 percent; 4. Communication and Network Security, 13 percent; 5. Identity and Access Management, 13 percent; 6. Security Assessment and Testing, 12 percent; 7. Security Operations, 13 percent; 8. Software Development Security, 10 percent. Verify the sum: 16 + 10 + 13 + 13 + 13 + 12 + 13 + 10 = 100. Computer-adaptive testing means the exam adjusts to you: answer correctly and the next question gets harder; answer incorrectly and it gets easier, until the algorithm converges on your ability level. Worked example of what CAT feels like. You answer three governance questions correctly; the exam then serves a harder scenario: 'A multinational must comply with conflicting data-retention laws in two jurisdictions while supporting a fraud investigation — what is the best approach?' That question is testing whether your ability holds at a higher difficulty, not whether you memorized a definition. Practical consequence: you cannot count questions or predict the end — the exam stops when it has measured you (between 100 and 150 questions) or time expires. Pacing: 3 hours for up to 150 questions is about 72 seconds per question at the maximum length, but most candidates finish with fewer questions; the discipline is the same flag-and-return method, with one CAT-specific rule — you generally cannot go back to earlier questions, so each answer must be committed with the mindset rules, not revisited. Common mistake: treating CISSP like a harder Security+. It is a different species: Security+ tests what you know, CISSP tests how you decide. The candidate who knows every port but answers like a technician ('fix it myself, fast') loses to the candidate who answers like a manager ('assess the risk, follow the process, protect the business'). One more CAT mechanic to internalize: because the exam adapts, early questions matter disproportionately - they set the difficulty trajectory. A confident, careful first twenty questions earns you harder questions, and harder questions are worth more in the adaptive scoring. The practical rule: slow down at the start. Read every stem twice, eliminate the technician's answer first, then choose the manager's answer. Candidates who rush the opening and then settle in have already told the algorithm they are weaker than they are. Second, the 'cannot go back' rule changes guessing strategy: on a linear exam you skip and return, but on CAT each answer is final - so apply the mindset rules decisively, commit, and move on. Lingering on a CAT question does not buy you a better answer; it buys you time pressure on the questions the algorithm still needs to measure you.
notes.title: The CISSP format: CAT testing and the eight-domain map

notes.body: The single biggest determinant of CISSP success is not knowledge — it is the mindset shift from technician to manager. CISSP's unofficial rules, repeated across every domain: human safety comes first (any scenario involving physical danger — fire, flood, injury — the correct answer protects people before property, data, or uptime); think like a manager (frame risk, follow process, document decisions, escalate properly); senior management owns security (ultimate accountability never sits with the technician); and security supports the business (controls that break the business are wrong answers). Worked example. Scenario: 'A critical database server is overheating and the cooling system has failed. The server hosts the order-processing system during peak sales.' The technician's answer: keep it running, point a fan at it, save the sales. The CISSP answer: shut it down in an orderly fashion — protecting the equipment and the facility (and the people near it) outranks revenue, and the business-continuity plan exists precisely for this moment. The exam is testing whether you know that availability never outranks safety. Second worked example. Scenario: 'You discover a colleague has been accessing salary records without authorization.' The technician's answer: confront the colleague, lock the account yourself. The manager's answer: follow the incident-response and HR process — document, report through proper channels, preserve evidence. CISSP punishes vigilantism and rewards process. Common mistake: choosing the fastest technical fix. On CISSP, 'fast' is suspicious — the correct answers are usually 'assess first,' 'follow the plan,' 'document the decision,' and 'get management approval.' Another trap: answers that are technically true but managerially wrong. 'Encrypt the database' is technically sound advice, but if the question asks what the CISO should do FIRST about a data-classification gap, the answer is 'establish the classification policy' — governance before technology, every time. Drill this until it is reflex: when two answers are both defensible, pick the one a prudent manager would choose, not the one a clever engineer would choose. A third worked example - the 'two right answers' drill. Scenario: 'A developer asks for production database access to debug a customer issue.' Answer A: 'Grant read-only access for today.' Answer B: 'Deny and require the ticket to go through the data-access approval process with masked data.' The technician picks A (fast, helpful, read-only feels safe). The CISSP answer is B: governance before convenience - the approval process exists to weigh the risk, and production data in debugging is an asset-security question, not a favor. The exam constructs these pairs constantly: the quick helpful answer vs. the process answer. Train the reflex: when you see the pair, the process answer wins unless human safety is at stake - in which case the safety answer beats everything. A second mindset anchor: 'the business decides.' CISSP never lets the technician make the business's risk decision. Your job in every scenario is to frame the risk, present options with costs, and let leadership choose - then execute faithfully. Candidates who 'decide for the business' fail even when their technical judgment was sound.
notes.title: The mindset shift: think like a manager, protect people first

notes.body: Domains 1 and 2 are the governance foundation the other six assume. Domain 1, Security and Risk Management (16 percent — the heaviest domain), covers security governance principles, risk management concepts, policies and standards, legal and regulatory issues, and business continuity. This is where the exam tests whether you understand that security is a business function: risk assessments drive control selection, policies drive behavior, and laws drive notification and liability decisions. Domain 2, Asset Security (10 percent), covers information and asset classification, ownership roles, handling requirements, and data retention and destruction. Worked example — classification driving everything. A company classifies data as Public, Internal, Confidential, and Restricted. The customer database is classified Confidential. From that single decision flow the handling rules: encryption at rest and in transit, access limited to the finance and support roles, no storage on removable media, retention of seven years per the legal schedule, and destruction by cryptographic erasure. An exam scenario will give you the classification and ask for the handling — or give you the mishandling and ask what failed first (answer: the classification process, because protection without classification is guessing). Second worked example — ownership roles. The marketing director (data owner) decides who may access the campaign database and approves the access policy; the IT team (data custodian) implements the access controls and maintains the system; the users (data subjects in privacy contexts) are the people the data describes. The classic trap asks who 'owns' the server — the custodian maintains it, but the owner decides its data's fate. Common mistake: answering Domain 1 questions with Domain 7 tools. When the scenario is 'the board asks whether the security budget is adequate,' the answer involves risk assessment and metrics, not 'deploy EDR.' Governance questions want governance answers. A third worked example - the legal/regulatory discriminator. Scenario: 'A company operating in the EU suffers a breach of customer data.' The Domain 1 concepts in play: breach-notification duties under GDPR (the exam expects you to know that notification obligations exist and are time-bound, without demanding exact hour counts from memory), the need for legal counsel before public statements, and evidence preservation for potential investigation. The CISSP-correct sequence: contain, engage legal, preserve evidence, notify per the applicable regulation's process. The trap answers are 'notify customers immediately on social media' (legal reviews first) and 'delete the attacker artifacts to clean up' (destroys evidence). A second Domain 2 drill: data retention. 'The legal team requires financial records kept seven years; the privacy team wants minimal retention.' The resolution: the data owner balances the requirements in the retention policy - legal hold overrides deletion schedules, and the policy documents the decision. The exam loves these tension scenarios; the answer is always the documented policy decision, not either extreme.
notes.title: Domains 1 and 2: governance, risk, and asset security (26% combined)

notes.body: Domains 3, 4, and 5 are the technical core — 39 percent combined — but CISSP tests them through a design-and-decision lens, not a configuration lens. Domain 3, Security Architecture and Engineering (13 percent): security models (Bell-LaPadula for confidentiality, Biba for integrity, Clark-Wilson for well-formed transactions), evaluation criteria, cryptography concepts, physical security, and secure design principles (least privilege, defense in depth, fail securely, economy of mechanism, complete mediation). Domain 4, Communication and Network Security (13 percent): secure network architecture and design, transmission media, network attacks and countermeasures, secure communications (VPNs, TLS, secure protocols). Domain 5, Identity and Access Management (13 percent): identification, authentication (single, multi-factor, and the factors themselves), authorization models (role-based, rule-based, mandatory, discretionary), and accountability (auditing, session management). Worked example — access model selection. Scenario: 'A defense contractor needs a system where access is determined by security clearance and data classification, enforced by the system regardless of user discretion.' That is mandatory access control (MAC) — the system enforces the policy (as in Bell-LaPadula's 'no read up, no write down' for confidentiality). Contrast: a company where managers grant access to their teams' folders is discretionary access control (DAC); a hospital where access follows job function is role-based (RBAC). The exam loves these three-way discriminations — memorize the one-sentence discriminator for each. Second worked example — fail securely. 'A firewall's primary power supply fails during an attack.' The secure design answer: the firewall fails closed (deny all) on its redundant supply or fails over to its HA peer — never fails open, because fail-open during an attack is the attacker winning by power outage. Common mistakes: confusing authentication (proving who you are) with authorization (what you are allowed to do) — the exam separates them relentlessly; and confusing Biba (integrity: no read down, no write up) with Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality: no read up, no write down) — learn them as mirror images. A third worked example - crypto concepts at the CISSP level. Scenario: 'Two parties need to exchange sensitive design documents with confidentiality, integrity, and non-repudiation.' The CISSP answer: encrypt with the recipient's public key (confidentiality - only the private-key holder reads it), sign with the sender's private key (non-repudiation and authenticity), and the recipient verifies the signature with the sender's public key and hashes the document (integrity). The exam tests whether you can assemble the primitives into a solution, not whether you can do the math. The classic trap: 'encrypt with your private key for confidentiality' - wrong, because anyone with your public key can decrypt it; private-key operations prove identity (signing), public-key operations protect confidentiality. A second network-security discriminator: the exam separates secure protocols from their insecure ancestors relentlessly - SSH replaces Telnet, HTTPS replaces HTTP, SFTP/FTPS replace FTP. When a scenario shows Telnet or FTP in use, the finding is the protocol, and the fix is its secure replacement.
notes.title: Domains 3, 4, and 5: architecture, networks, and IAM (39% combined)

notes.body: Domains 6, 7, and 8 close the loop: verify, operate, and build securely. Domain 6, Security Assessment and Testing (12 percent): test strategies, security control testing, vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, audits, and log reviews — the exam tests whether you know which assessment fits which question. Domain 7, Security Operations (13 percent): the SOC world — investigations, logging and monitoring, provisioning, incident management, disaster recovery — but at the management level: are the processes defined, measured, and improving? Domain 8, Software Development Security (10 percent): SDLC security, secure coding, maturity models, databases and data warehousing security. Worked example — assessment selection. Scenario: 'Management wants to know whether the company's access controls are operating effectively across all departments.' The answer is an audit (or security assessment) — a broad evaluation against a standard — not a penetration test (which is a narrow, adversarial test of specific systems) and not a vulnerability scan (which finds technical weaknesses without testing control effectiveness). The discriminator: audits answer 'are we doing what we said?'; pen tests answer 'can an attacker break this specific thing?'; vuln scans answer 'what weaknesses exist?' Second worked example — SDLC root cause. 'A web application ships the same injection vulnerability in three consecutive releases.' The Domain 8 answer: the SDLC lacks secure-coding standards, code review, and security testing gates — patching each release treats the symptom; fixing the development process treats the disease. Common mistakes: recommending a penetration test when the scenario asks for control effectiveness (that is an audit); and answering operations questions with heroics ('work all weekend to rebuild') instead of process ('invoke the disaster-recovery plan, which defines RTO/RPO and roles'). On CISSP, the plan is always the answer — preparation beats improvisation, and the exam rewards the candidate who trusts the process. A third worked example - the SDLC gate question. Scenario: 'A company wants to stop injection flaws from reaching production.' The Domain 8 answer is a set of SDLC gates: secure-coding standards, automated static analysis in the pipeline, mandatory peer code review for data-access code, and dynamic testing in staging - with a policy that blocks release when gates fail. Patching production after each incident is the wrong answer (treats symptoms); the gates treat the disease. The exam's discriminator: any answer choice that fixes the process beats any choice that fixes the instance. A second Domain 6 drill: 'The audit committee wants assurance that the new access-control system works as designed.' The answer is a controls assessment against the requirements - not a pen test (which would test whether an attacker can bypass it, a different question). The exam separates 'does it work as designed' (assessment/audit) from 'can it be broken' (pen test) from 'what weaknesses exist' (vuln scan) with near-religious consistency. Memorize the three questions each answers and you will not miss these.
notes.title: Domains 6, 7, and 8: assess, operate, build securely (35% combined)

notes.body: A CISSP study plan is a management exercise in itself: allocate by weight, drill the mindset, and measure with scenarios. Phase 1 — foundations (weeks 1-3): Domains 1 and 2 plus the mindset rules. Read governance and risk material until you can explain risk responses (avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept) and ownership roles without notes; write your personal list of the top 10 CISSP mindset rules. Phase 2 — technical core (weeks 4-7): Domains 3, 4, and 5. Build comparison tables: Bell-LaPadula vs. Biba vs. Clark-Wilson; MAC vs. DAC vs. RBAC; symmetric vs. asymmetric crypto concepts; network attacks vs. countermeasures. Phase 3 — verification and operations (weeks 8-9): Domains 6, 7, and 8. Drill assessment-type selection and SDLC security until the discriminators are instant. Phase 4 — integration (weeks 10-12): full scenario sets only, timed, with the decision log. Worked example — the decision log in action. Question: 'A new regulation requires breach notification within 72 hours. The current incident-response plan has no notification procedure. What should the CISO do first?' Tempting technical answer: 'Buy a breach-notification tool.' Correct management answer: 'Update the incident-response plan and assign notification responsibilities.' Decision-log entry: 'Governance before technology — the plan defines the duty; the tool only executes it.' Twenty such entries rewire your reflexes from engineer to manager. The CISSP practice gate: timed scenario sets of 40 questions in 75 minutes, scored by domain, with the gate at 75 percent overall and no domain below 60 percent. Because CAT adapts, your practice must include hard questions — if every practice question feels easy, you are not training at the difficulty the exam will actually serve you. Operator gotcha: experienced technicians fail CISSP by overthinking technical minutiae and underweighting the management answer. When you catch yourself debating cipher modes on a question whose stem is about policy, stop — the stem's first sentence tells you which domain (and which mindset) owns the question. A second worked example - the decision log catching a drift. Midway through Phase 4 you notice your log shows five entries where you picked the technical answer over the management one - all in Domain 7 scenarios about 'restoring service fast.' The pattern reveals your bias: under operations pressure you revert to technician. The fix is a personal rule added to the log's front page: 'In Domain 7, the plan is the answer - invoke the procedure before improvising.' Two weeks later the same scenario type appears and you pick the management answer without hesitation. That is the decision log working as a bias-correction instrument, not just a notebook. A final exam-week protocol: stop new material five days out; run only timed scenario sets and decision-log reviews. Sleep eight hours the last three nights - CAT punishes fatigue more than linear exams do, because every question demands judgment, and judgment is the first casualty of tiredness.

handsOnLab.brief: You will build a real open-book index for your GSEC notes: a tabbed, term-to-page reference system, then prove it works with timed lookup drills and a full practice gate.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Two consecutive timed lookup drills complete 20 lookups in under 30 minutes with 90%+ accuracy, and your practice gate scores 80%+ with the index.
handsOnLab.deliverable: gsec-index/ folder with index.md (term-to-page map), tabs-plan.md, lookup-drill-log.md, and gate-scorecard.md.
steps: Create gsec-index/ with index.md, tabs-plan.md, lookup-drill-log.md, gate-scorecard.md.
In tabs-plan.md, define your tab categories: crypto, access control, Windows security, Linux security, network security, incident handling, risk/governance.
In index.md, build the term-to-page map: every key term from this module's notes mapped to its location (note number + page/section).
Add cross-references: link related terms (e.g., 'least privilege -> access control -> elevation control').
Run lookup drill 1: have a partner (or a random-term script) call out 20 terms; find each in the index and record the time in lookup-drill-log.md.
Tune the index: every term that took over 60 seconds gets a better entry or an additional cross-reference.
Run lookup drill 2 with 20 fresh terms; the gate is 20 lookups in under 30 minutes at 90%+ accuracy.
Build a 50-question practice set weighted to GSEC essentials topics and run it open-book in 2 hours.
Score it in gate-scorecard.md with per-topic breakdowns.
For every miss, decide: index gap (fix the index), knowledge gap (study the topic), or lookup-time casualty (drill more).
Repeat the gate on a fresh set until you score 80%+ twice in a row.
