notes.body: Zero trust is the philosophy behind every ThreatLocker module, and the panel will expect you to speak it fluently — not as a slogan, but as operational reasoning. The principles: never trust, always verify (no implicit trust based on network location — inside the LAN is not safe); assume breach (design as if the attacker is already inside); verify explicitly (authenticate and authorize every access decision with all available signals); least privilege (every identity and process gets the minimum access it needs, nothing more); and microsegmentation (divide the environment so a compromise cannot move laterally). Worked example — the panel classic. 'Why is zero trust better than a strong perimeter?' Your 60-second answer: 'A perimeter assumes everything inside is trustworthy, so one breached workstation means the whole LAN is exposed — the attacker moves laterally at will. Zero trust removes that assumption: every application launch is verified against policy (allowlisting), every application's capabilities are constrained (ringfencing), no user holds standing admin (elevation control), storage and network access are granted per-policy (storage and network control). The 2026 reality is that phishing beats perimeters weekly; zero trust assumes the phish succeeded and still contains the damage.' Second worked example — mapping principles to modules for the panel. Never-trust-always-verify becomes allowlisting (verify every executable). Least privilege becomes elevation control (no standing admin) plus ringfencing (apps get minimum capability). Assume breach becomes network control (dynamic ACLs limit lateral movement) plus Detect (alert on what the modules block). Microsegmentation becomes network control policies per endpoint. When the panel asks 'what does zero trust mean to you,' answer with the principles AND the module mapping — concept plus operation is what separates a candidate who read the website from one who can do the job. Common mistake: describing zero trust as a product you buy. It is an architecture and a discipline; ThreatLocker's modules are enforcement mechanisms for it. The panel wants operators who understand the philosophy deeply enough to make policy decisions, not recite marketing. TECHNICAL BANK 1 — zero trust: Q1: 'Define zero trust in one sentence.' A: 'A security model that eliminates implicit trust and verifies every access decision explicitly, assuming breach.' Q2: 'Why does network location no longer imply trust?' A: 'Phishing, VPN compromises, and insider threats routinely place attackers inside the perimeter; location is not identity.' Q3: 'How does least privilege limit ransomware?' A: 'Ransomware inherits the privileges of its host process; standard-user execution plus no standing admin blocks persistence and lateral movement.' Q4: 'What is microsegmentation's goal?' A: 'Contain breaches by dividing the environment so compromise of one segment cannot reach others.' Q5: 'Name the five principles.' A: 'Never trust always verify, assume breach, verify explicitly, least privilege, microsegmentation.'
notes.title: Zero-trust concepts: the philosophy the panel expects you to speak

notes.body: Allowlisting (Application Control) is ThreatLocker's deny-by-default core: it learns the application environment, permits what users use, and denies everything else. Understand the inversion deeply, because the panel will probe it: traditional antivirus is default-allow with blocklists — everything runs unless it matches a known-bad signature, so novel malware walks through. Allowlisting is default-deny — nothing runs unless it is known-good, so novel malware is stopped without anyone needing to recognize it. The learning phase matters operationally: on deployment, the platform observes the environment to learn which applications users actually run, and policy is built from that observed reality — then enforcement denies everything outside it. Worked example — the panel scenario. 'A customer asks why their new accounting tool was blocked.' Your answer: 'Allowlisting denied it because it was not in the learned permitted set — that is the system working as designed. The workflow is: verify the tool is legitimate and approved, add it to policy through the proper change process, and it runs. The block is not an error; it is the default-deny guarantee. If we allowed unknown executables while we checked, we would not have allowlisting.' Second worked example — the zero-day question. 'How does allowlisting stop malware nobody has seen before?' Answer: 'It does not need to see it. The malware is an unknown executable, and unknown executables do not run — full stop. Signature-based tools must recognize the threat; allowlisting only needs to recognize the permitted set, which is finite and known.' Common mistake: confusing allowlisting with whitelisting-as-a-list you maintain by hand. The operational reality is learning plus policy: the platform learns the environment, policy codifies the decisions, and changes flow through approval — not through a spreadsheet someone edits. Another trap: promising the panel that allowlisting 'stops all malware.' The honest operator answer: it stops unauthorized execution, which kills the vast majority of malware delivery — and ringfencing, elevation control, and network control cover what execution alone cannot. TECHNICAL BANK 2 — allowlisting: Q6: 'Default-allow vs default-deny in one sentence each.' A: 'Default-allow runs everything except known-bad; default-deny runs only known-good.' Q7: 'What happens during the learning phase?' A: 'The platform observes which applications the environment actually uses, so policy reflects operational reality.' Q8: 'A legitimate new app is blocked. Is this a failure?' A: 'No — it is default-deny working. Verify, approve through change control, add to policy.' Q9: 'Why does allowlisting not need malware signatures?' A: 'It evaluates the executable against the permitted set, not against a threat database.' Q10: 'What is the operator's job in an allowlisting deployment?' A: 'Learn the environment, build policy from observed use, handle approval requests, and audit the permitted set.'
notes.title: Allowlisting operations: deny-by-default, done right

notes.body: Ringfencing is the module the panel will press hardest on, because it is ThreatLocker's distinctive answer to the hardest problem in endpoint security: the trusted application turned weapon. Ringfencing restricts what allowed applications can do — it can block them from executing other applications or processes, editing the registry, reading or writing files, and opening network sessions. The threat model: the application itself is legitimate and permitted (Word, a browser, a line-of-business app), but an attacker exploits it — a malicious document, a drive-by, a macro — and uses the trusted app as the launchpad. Without ringfencing, the trusted app's privileges become the attacker's privileges. With ringfencing, the app runs but its capabilities are caged. Worked example — the canonical scenario. A user opens a Word document with a malicious macro. Word is allowed; the macro tries to launch PowerShell to download a payload. Ringfencing blocks Word from executing other processes — the attack dies at the launch attempt, and Detect logs the blocked indicator. Your panel answer: 'The document opened, the user saw no disruption, the weaponization was stopped, and we have the forensic record.' Second worked example — the business-app dilemma. A customer's legacy application is required for operations but has a known history of exploitation. Uninstalling is not an option; allowing it unrestricted is not acceptable. The operator's answer: permit the application via allowlisting (it is known-good and needed), then ringfence it aggressively — no child processes, no registry writes, no unexpected network sessions, file access limited to its working directories. The business keeps its app; the attacker loses every weaponization path. That tradeoff reasoning — security without breaking operations — is exactly what the IT Infrastructure Specialist role does daily. Common mistake: describing ringfencing as 'blocking bad apps.' It constrains good apps. The exam-style discriminator: allowlisting decides WHAT runs; ringfencing decides what running things MAY DO. Memorize that sentence — it answers half the module-confusion questions. TECHNICAL BANK 3 — ringfencing: Q11: 'What does ringfencing restrict?' A: 'The capabilities of allowed applications: executing other processes, registry edits, file read/write, network sessions.' Q12: 'Word launches PowerShell via macro. What happens?' A: 'Ringfencing blocks the child-process execution; Detect logs the blocked indicator.' Q13: 'Allowlisting vs ringfencing in one line.' A: 'Allowlisting decides what runs; ringfencing decides what running things may do.' Q14: 'A required legacy app has known exploits. Your recommendation?' A: 'Allowlist it as known-good and needed, then ringfence its capabilities tightly.' Q15: 'Does ringfencing break the application?' A: 'Properly scoped, no — it constrains capabilities the app does not legitimately need.'
notes.title: Ringfencing scenarios: caging the trusted app

notes.body: Elevation Control solves the oldest tension in Windows operations: users and applications periodically need administrative rights, but standing local admin is how malware gains the keys to the kingdom. The module removes local admin from endpoints and replaces it with just-in-time elevation delegated to applications via policy — the application gets the elevation it needs, when it needs it, without the user ever holding administrative privilege. Worked example — the legacy app problem. A line-of-business application requires administrative rights to update itself. The old world: make the user a local admin (and hand every malware process on that box admin rights too). The Elevation Control world: policy grants that specific application just-in-time elevation for its updater — the update runs elevated, the user stays standard, malware in the user's context stays unprivileged. Your panel answer walks that contrast explicitly, because it shows you understand both the operational pain and the security win. Second worked example — the help-desk ticket. 'I need admin to install the approved printer driver.' The operator's workflow: verify the request and the software's legitimacy, apply the elevation policy for that installer (time-bound, application-scoped), the install completes, elevation expires. No standing admin granted, no ticket ping-pong, full audit trail of what elevated and when. Common mistake: describing elevation control as 'blocking admin tasks.' It enables them — safely. The panel wants to hear that you understand the user-experience side: security that breaks workflows gets bypassed, and bypassed security is no security. The winning framing is always 'the user gets their work done, the attacker gets nothing.' A second trap: confusing elevation control with allowlisting. Allowlisting decides the updater may run; elevation control decides it may run elevated. They compose — and explaining how they compose shows operator-grade understanding. TECHNICAL BANK 4 — elevation control: Q16: 'What does Elevation Control remove?' A: 'Standing local admin rights from endpoints.' Q17: 'How does a legitimate app get admin when it needs it?' A: 'Just-in-time elevation delegated to the application via policy.' Q18: 'Why is removing local admin a malware control?' A: 'Malware inherits its host's privileges; standard-user context blocks persistence and system-wide changes.' Q19: 'User needs admin for one installer. The workflow?' A: 'Verify, apply time-bound application-scoped elevation policy, install completes, elevation expires.' Q20: 'Elevation Control vs allowlisting?' A: 'Allowlisting decides what runs; Elevation Control decides with what privilege it runs.' One more panel nuance: when asked about elevation, always mention the audit trail - every just-in-time elevation is logged with the application, the time, and the policy that granted it. Panels love the accountability angle: least privilege plus full visibility is the complete answer. And connect it to the hiring logic: the IT Infrastructure Specialist who can explain WHY the control exists (malware inherits privilege) and HOW it preserves workflow (the app elevates, the user does not) is demonstrating exactly the operator-plus-communicator blend the role demands.
notes.title: Elevation Control: least privilege without breaking workflows

notes.body: Storage Control applies granular policy to the storage layer: storage devices, file paths, and shares. Its job is blocking data theft and exfiltration — the insider with a USB drive, the malware staging files for theft, the misconfigured share exposing regulated data. The granularity is the point: policy can distinguish device classes (block USB mass storage while permitting USB keyboards and mice), paths (protect the customer-data directory regardless of who touches it), and shares (control who can read or write the finance share, and from where). Worked example — the insider scenario. An employee plugs in a personal USB drive and drags the customer database onto it. Storage Control policy blocks writes to removable mass storage for that data classification — the copy fails, Detect logs the attempt with the indicator, and the SOC has the forensic record. Your panel answer: 'The theft was prevented at the storage layer, before the data left the building, with an auditable event.' Second worked example — the ransomware-adjacent scenario. Malware attempts to stage encrypted archives in a temp directory for exfiltration before detonating. Path-based policy denies the staging writes; the exfiltration step fails even if the malware executed. This is defense in depth at the data layer — network control may catch the C2, but storage control catches the data movement itself. Common mistake: describing storage control as 'USB blocking.' Device control is one facet; path and share policy are the deeper story, and the panel will respect the candidate who leads with data-centric policy rather than device anecdotes. Another nuance: storage policy must be designed around data classification — you protect paths by what the data IS, not by which user touched it last. That data-centric framing connects directly to governance concepts and shows maturity beyond tool operation. TECHNICAL BANK 5 — storage control: Q21: 'What three things does Storage Control govern?' A: 'Storage devices, file paths, and shares.' Q22: 'Block USB drives but allow USB keyboards. How?' A: 'Device-class policy: deny USB mass storage, permit HID devices.' Q23: 'An insider copies the customer DB to USB. What happens?' A: 'Path/device policy blocks the write; Detect logs the blocked attempt.' Q24: 'Why path-based policy instead of user-based?' A: 'Protection follows the data's classification, not whoever touched it last.' Q25: 'How does Storage Control complement Network Control against exfiltration?' A: 'Storage Control stops the data movement; Network Control stops the C2 channel — two layers, one attack.'
notes.title: Storage Control: guarding data at rest and in motion

notes.body: Network Control is the endpoint firewall with dynamic ACLs — access control lists that open and close ports as policy dictates, rather than the static port rules of a traditional firewall. Its operational jobs: block lateral movement (an infected host cannot probe its neighbors), block command-and-control (beaconing out to attacker infrastructure dies at the endpoint), and enforce least-privilege networking per application and per endpoint. The 'dynamic' part matters for the panel: ports open when policy permits the legitimate traffic and close otherwise, shrinking the window in which an attacker can use them. Worked example — the lateral-movement scenario. Malware lands on one workstation and begins scanning the subnet for SMB shares to infect. Network Control policy denies workstation-to-workstation SMB — the scan hits a wall at the first neighbor, Detect logs the blocked attempts, and the incident is one host instead of fifty. Your panel answer: 'The blast radius stayed at one because the endpoint firewall enforced segmentation the network firewall could not see.' Second worked example — the C2 scenario. An endpoint begins beaconing to a newly registered domain every 60 seconds. Network Control blocks the outbound sessions per policy; Detect fires alerts on the blocked indicators of compromise, giving the SOC the domain, the cadence, and the affected host. The analyst's next moves — isolate, image, hunt for siblings — start from that alert. Common mistake: describing network control as 'a firewall.' Every endpoint has a firewall; the operator story is dynamic, policy-driven ACLs plus the Detect telemetry loop. The panel wants to hear the loop: block, alert, investigate, tune. A second trap: forgetting that network control is also a usability story — legitimate applications get the ports they need via policy, so the business keeps working while the attacker starves. TECHNICAL BANK 6 — network control: Q26: 'What makes the ACLs dynamic?' A: 'They open and close ports per policy rather than holding static rules.' Q27: 'How does Network Control limit lateral movement?' A: 'Endpoint firewall policy denies host-to-host traffic like workstation SMB scans.' Q28: 'Beaconing to a new domain every 60 seconds. The response?' A: 'Network Control blocks the sessions; Detect alerts on the blocked IOCs; the analyst isolates and hunts.' Q29: 'Network Control vs the perimeter firewall?' A: 'The perimeter guards the boundary; Network Control enforces policy at every endpoint, including inside the LAN.' Q30: 'Does blocking ports break legitimate apps?' A: 'Policy permits what the business needs — the attacker starves while operations continue.'
notes.title: Network Control: dynamic ACLs and the lateral-movement kill chain

notes.body: ThreatLocker Detect is the telemetry and alerting layer: it alerts on indicators of compromise that the modules block. Understand its role precisely — Detect does not prevent (the modules do that); it informs. Every blocked execution, every caged capability, every denied exfiltration attempt, every killed C2 session becomes an alert with context: what was blocked, which module blocked it, which endpoint, which user, when. That context is what makes the SOC workflow possible. The triage discipline for any Detect alert: verify (is this a true positive? check the indicator against intel and the endpoint's baseline), scope (is it one host or many? search for sibling indicators), contain (isolate the host, disable the account, block the IOC at the perimeter too), document (timeline, actions, evidence preserved), then decide (tune the policy, escalate to incident response, or close as benign with rationale). Worked example — the 2 AM alert. Detect fires: Ringfencing blocked winword.exe from launching powershell.exe on WS-114, user jdoe, 02:14. Verify: the document came from an external sender, the macro hash matches a known malicious sample — true positive. Scope: search Detect for the same document hash and parent-child pattern across the fleet — two more hosts, same hour. Contain: isolate all three, disable the accounts, block the sender domain at the gateway. Document: timeline and IOCs to the ticket. Decide: escalate to full incident response — this is a campaign, not an isolated event. Your panel answer walks exactly that chain, because the panel is testing whether you think in workflows or in single alerts. Second worked example — the false positive. Detect alerts on a blocked installer: the software is legitimate, the vendor just changed its signing certificate. Verify: confirm with the vendor and the change ticket. Decide: update the allowlisting policy for the new certificate, document the exception, close. The discipline is identical — only the verdict differs — and saying so shows the panel you do not cry wolf. Common mistake: treating Detect as the protection. The modules protect; Detect narrates. The operator who confuses the two will misanswer 'what stopped the attack' (the module) vs. 'how did you know' (Detect). TECHNICAL BANK 7 — Detect triage: Q31: 'What does Detect do?' A: 'Alerts on indicators of compromise blocked by the ThreatLocker modules.' Q32: 'Walk a Detect alert triage.' A: 'Verify, scope, contain, document, then tune, escalate, or close.' Q33: 'Ringfencing blocks Word launching PowerShell at 2 AM. First move?' A: 'Verify: check the document source and macro hash — confirm true positive before containing.' Q34: 'Same pattern on three hosts. What changed?' A: 'Scope says campaign — escalate to full incident response, not a single-host ticket.' Q35: 'A blocked installer turns out legitimate. The workflow?' A: 'Verify with vendor and change ticket, update policy for the new certificate, document, close.'
notes.title: ThreatLocker Detect triage: from alert to action

notes.body: The panel will also test generalist infrastructure skill — Windows endpoint troubleshooting and networking fundamentals — because the IT Infrastructure Specialist supports the whole endpoint, not just the ThreatLocker agent. Windows troubleshooting order: check Event Viewer (System and Application logs) for the error and its timestamp, check the application's own logs, verify recent changes (updates, GPO, agent installs), reproduce the issue, and escalate with the evidence bundle. Networking fundamentals: the bottom-up order — physical (cable, link lights, Wi-Fi association), IP configuration (ipconfig: address, mask, gateway, DNS), gateway reachability (ping the gateway), DNS resolution (nslookup), then the service itself (port check, application log). Memorize the discriminators: 'can ping 8.8.8.8 but cannot browse' is DNS; '169.254.x.x address' is DHCP failure (APIPA); 'works on Wi-Fi but not Ethernet' is the wired path (cable, switch port, NIC). Worked example — the post-agent-install ticket. 'After the ThreatLocker agent was installed, the accounting app cannot sync.' Your troubleshooting: confirm the app worked before (isolate the change), check Detect for blocked indicators from that app (is a module denying it?), check Ringfencing policy on the app (blocked child process or network session?), check Network Control (needed port closed?), then resolve via policy — not by disabling the agent. The panel loves this scenario because the wrong answer ('uninstall the agent') trades security for convenience, and the right answer fixes it with policy. Second worked example — the interview-day scoring rubric you will hold yourself to. Per question, 6 points: accuracy (0-2: correct facts, correct module, correct reasoning), structure (0-2: what, why, operational implication — in that order), concision (0-1: 60-90 seconds, then stop), honesty (0-1: 'I don't know, but here is how I would find out' beats an invented fact — inventing facts is an automatic zero for the question). Forty questions at 6 points is 240; the gate is 85 percent (204). The honesty rule is the most important: panels forgive 'I don't know,' they never forgive bluffing. TECHNICAL BANK 8 — troubleshooting and fundamentals: Q36: 'Workstation cannot reach the file server. Order?' A: 'Physical, ipconfig, ping gateway, nslookup/DNS, then the service.' Q37: 'Can ping 8.8.8.8, cannot browse. Diagnosis?' A: 'DNS failure — nslookup to confirm, then check DNS server config.' Q38: '169.254.x.x address. What failed?' A: 'DHCP — no lease; check DHCP server, relay, and link.' Q39: 'App crashes on one workstation only. First look?' A: 'Event Viewer Application log, then the app's own logs.' Q40: 'App breaks after agent install. The wrong fix and the right fix?' A: 'Wrong: disable the agent. Right: check Detect and module policy, resolve via policy.'

drills.title: Delivery coaching — rapid fire

handsOnLab.brief: You will build your personal STAR bank: 15 prompts, each with two real story scaffolds filled from YOUR history only, every story rehearsed aloud and timed at 60-90 seconds.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: All 15 prompts have two real scaffolds each, every story is timed at 60-90 seconds aloud, and a reviewer (or recording) confirms zero invented details.
handsOnLab.deliverable: star-bank/ folder with prompts.md (15 prompts), stories.md (30 real scaffolds), rehearsal-log.md (timings per story), and panel-day-checklist.md.
steps: Create star-bank/ with prompts.md, stories.md, rehearsal-log.md, panel-day-checklist.md.
In prompts.md, write all 15 behavioral prompts from this module's notes, numbered.
In stories.md, create two scaffold slots per prompt — 30 slots total — each with S/T/A/R headings left BLANK.
Fill each slot with YOUR real history only: real situations, real tasks, real actions, real measured results.
Apply the honesty audit: for every story, ask 'did this really happen, in these details?' Delete or correct anything uncertain.
Time each story ALOUD with a stopwatch; record the time in rehearsal-log.md. Target: 60-90 seconds each.
Cut or expand stories to fit the window: one incident, action chain, quantified result.
Rehearse the full bank aloud twice; mark every story pass/fail on timing and completeness.
In panel-day-checklist.md, write your Oct 13 plan: arrival time, documents, 2-3 questions for the panel, and your opening/closing lines.
Do a final full-bank rehearsal the evening of Oct 12 — warm-up, not new material.
Morning of Oct 13: review the checklist only. Trust the rehearsal.
handsOnLab.title: Build your STAR bank: 30 real stories, timed and rehearsed

notes.body: STAR is the structure every behavioral answer needs: Situation (the specific incident — one event, not your career), Task (what you were responsible for — the mission you owned), Action (what YOU did, step by step, in first person), Result (the measurable outcome — numbers, time, money, satisfaction). The panel asks behavioral questions because past behavior predicts future performance, and STAR is how you make your past legible in 60 to 90 seconds. Worked example — a scaffold with placeholders, NOT a real story. S: '[A real 2 AM alert you triaged — name the system and the symptom.]' T: '[What you owned that night — triage, containment, communication.]' A: '[Your exact steps in order: verified the alert, scoped the fleet, isolated the hosts, documented the timeline.]' R: '[Measured outcome: contained in X minutes, Y hosts affected, playbook updated with Z change.]' Notice the discipline: every bracket is a prompt for YOUR real history. The scaffold teaches the shape; only your life fills it. Nothing in this module invents your history — any example that looks like a story is a labeled scaffold with empty brackets, and your lab work is filling those brackets truthfully. Second worked example — the timing math. Ninety seconds at conversational pace is roughly 180-220 words: about 40 words for Situation, 30 for Task, 90 for Action, 40 for Result. The Action gets the most words because the panel is hiring your judgment under pressure — what you did, in what order, and why. Practice with a stopwatch until the shape is muscle memory: when nerves hit on Oct 13, the four beats give you rails. Common mistake: spending 60 seconds on the Situation. The panel does not need the company's history — it needs the incident, your mission, your moves, and the score. A second classic: 'we' instead of 'I.' Team context gets 'we'; every action beat gets 'I.' If your Action paragraph has zero first-person verbs, rewrite it. A third worked example - the 90-second budget as a rehearsal tool. Record yourself answering one scaffold aloud, then transcribe it and count the words per beat. Typical first attempts: 100 words of Situation, 20 of Task, 60 of Action, 10 of Result - the exact inversion of the ideal. The transcription does not lie, and one round of it fixes the shape permanently: cut the Situation to the incident, expand the Action to your steps, and give the Result its numbers. A second timing trick: the headline. Open every answer with a one-sentence headline ('I contained a three-host incident in 20 minutes') before the STAR detail. The headline buys you the panel's attention for the remaining 75 seconds - and if nerves ever cut an answer short, the headline alone still landed the point. Practice headlines separately: one sentence per story, specific and quantified, until they are automatic.
notes.title: STAR refresher: the four beats and the 90-second shape

notes.body: Delivery is half the score. The coaching rules: lead with the headline ('I contained a three-host malware incident in 20 minutes'), then STAR the detail — panels remember structured answers. Be specific: names of systems, exact steps, real numbers. Be quantified: minutes, percentages, counts — 'quickly' and 'better' are opinions, numbers are evidence. Be honest: if you have no direct story, say so and give the closest real one — fabrication collapses under follow-up questions, and interviewers ask follow-ups precisely to test whether the story is yours. End with the lesson when the prompt invites it ('what I changed afterward'), because growth stories beat hero stories. Worked example — the same scaffold delivered two ways. Weak: 'So there was this alert, and it was pretty bad, and we all jumped on it, and eventually we got it handled, and it was fine.' Strong: 'Detect fired at 2 AM on three hosts showing the same macro-malware pattern. I owned triage that night. I verified the true positive against the macro hash, searched the fleet for siblings, isolated all three hosts, and documented the timeline. We contained it in 20 minutes with no lateral movement, and I updated the playbook with the new indicator.' Same incident, different candidate — the strong version has a headline, first-person actions in order, and a measured result. Second worked example — handling the follow-up. Panel: 'What would you do differently?' Strong answer: 'I would have pulled the email gateway logs first — I spent ten minutes confirming what the gateway could have told me in two. I added that step to the playbook.' The follow-up is a gift: it lets you show self-awareness and process improvement, which is what senior interviewers are actually scoring. Common mistake: memorizing scripts word-for-word. Rehearse the beats and the numbers, not the sentences — memorized sentences sound robotic and shatter when the panel interrupts. Know your stories; speak them fresh each time. A third delivery scenario - the interrupted answer. Midway through your Action beat, a panelist interjects: 'Wait - why did you isolate before blocking the C2?' The wrong response is fluster and restart. The right response: answer the interjection directly ('Isolation stops lateral movement in seconds; the firewall block took two minutes to propagate - so isolation bought the containment window'), then bridge back ('...which is why the next step was the C2 block you asked about'). Interruptions are engagement, not attacks - the panelist is interested enough to dig. Welcome the dig: it lets you show the reasoning behind the steps, which is what senior interviewers score highest. A rehearsal method: have a partner interrupt every practice answer with one 'why' question. After a week of it, real interruptions feel like the practice - which is the entire point of rehearsal.
notes.title: Delivery coaching: specific, quantified, honest

notes.body: The support-flavored prompts test the Cyber Hero dimension of the role: customers, frustration, and service under pressure. Prompt 1: 'Tell me about a difficult customer or frustrated user you supported.' The panel wants de-escalation plus resolution — listen first, acknowledge the frustration without defensiveness, diagnose systematically, resolve, and follow up. Prompt 2: 'How do you handle a customer who is upset about a blocked application?' This is the ThreatLocker-specific version: the allowlisting block from M39 becomes a service interaction — explain the protection plainly, verify legitimacy, shepherd the approval, follow up when it is permitted. Prompt 3: 'Describe a time you had to say no to a request.' The panel tests backbone with empathy — the secure answer delivered kindly, with the alternative offered. For each prompt, build two scaffolds in your lab: S-[the real interaction], T-[what you owned], A-[your exact de-escalation and resolution steps], R-[measured outcome: resolution time, satisfaction, repeat-contact avoided]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 2 without inventing. S: '[A real time a security control blocked legitimate work.]' T: '[Your responsibility: resolve the block without weakening security.]' A: '[How you explained the block in plain language, verified the software, processed the approval, confirmed the fix with the user.]' R: '[Time to resolution, the user's response, any process improvement you suggested.]' The scaffold is complete and honest — and completely empty of invented facts. Your job in the lab is to fill it with one real memory. Common mistake: answering support prompts with pure technical detail. The panel is scoring the human interaction — lead with how you handled the person, then the technical resolution. A second trap: badmouthing the customer, even lightly. 'The user was being unreasonable' fails the prompt; 'the user was frustrated because their deadline was at risk, so I...' passes it. A fourth support prompt for the bank - Prompt 3b: 'How do you explain a technical problem to a non-technical person?' The Cyber Hero answer: analogies anchored in the user's world, no jargon, check for understanding, and the fix framed as what THEY need to do (one clear action). Scaffold: S-[a real explanation you gave], T-[what the user needed to understand or do], A-[your explanation approach: the analogy, the single action item, the confirmation], R-[the user succeeded / the ticket closed cleanly]. This prompt appears constantly in support-adjacent roles because it tests the rarest combination: deep technical understanding expressed simply. The trap is the expert's curse - explaining at YOUR level instead of theirs. The fix is the teach-back: 'just to make sure I explained it clearly, could you tell me what you will do next?' - which verifies understanding while respecting the user. Practice one teach-back line until it sounds natural, not scripted.
notes.title: Prompts 1-3: the difficult customer and the blocked app

notes.body: Pressure prompts test triage thinking: what you do first, what you defer, and how you communicate while the clock runs. Prompt 4: 'Describe a time you worked an outage or incident under pressure.' The panel wants the order of your thinking — verify, scope, contain, communicate — not just the fix. Prompt 5: 'Tell me about a time you had to make a quick decision with incomplete information.' Show the decision framework: what you knew, what you assumed, the reversible-vs-irreversible test, and what you did when new information arrived. Prompt 6: 'How do you prioritize when everything is urgent?' The answer is a real triage story: impact times urgency, communicated explicitly, with the deferrals named. Scaffold each with the pressure beats: S-[the real incident], T-[your role in the response], A-[your steps IN ORDER, including what you deliberately deferred], R-[restoration time, blast radius contained, lesson captured]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 5. S: '[A real decision you made with incomplete information.]' T: '[What was at stake and what you owned.]' A: '[What you knew, your key assumption, why you chose the reversible option first, how you updated when facts arrived.]' R: '[The outcome and what the decision taught you about deciding under uncertainty.]' Notice the A-beat includes the assumption explicitly — panels respect candidates who name their assumptions, because hidden assumptions are how incidents get worse. Common mistake: the hero narrative — 'I saved the day single-handedly.' Pressure stories that erase the team read as either fiction or arrogance. Name your part precisely and credit the team where it contributed: 'I owned triage; a colleague handled comms; we restored service in 40 minutes.' Precision about your role is more impressive than inflation of it. A second trap: skipping the communication beat. Under pressure, telling people what is happening IS part of the job — stakeholders, users, the next shift. If your A-beat has no communication step, add one from your real memory. A fourth pressure prompt - Prompt 6b: 'Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision during an incident.' The panel tests whether you can dissent productively under load: state the disagreement crisply, propose the alternative with its tradeoff, accept the call once made, and execute fully. Scaffold: S-[the real incident and the decision], T-[your role and what you saw differently], A-[how you raised it: the data, the alternative, the acceptance], R-[the outcome and what the team learned about dissent]. The scoring: loyalty to the decision after it is made matters as much as the courage to raise the concern. 'I argued, lost, then slow-walked the plan' fails catastrophically; 'I argued with data, the lead chose otherwise, I executed fully, and we debriefed after' passes cleanly. Panels ask this because incident dissent handled badly destroys teams - show them you strengthen the team instead.
notes.title: Prompts 4-6: outage, decisions, and triage under pressure

notes.body: The mistake prompt is the integrity test — every panel asks it, and it is the easiest prompt to fail by being too polished. Prompt 7: 'Tell me about a mistake you made at work.' The scoring is entirely about accountability: name it plainly, own it fully, show the fix, and show what changed in your process afterward. The mistake itself should be real and proportionate — not catastrophic (which raises judgment questions) and not trivial (which reads as evasion). Prompt 8: 'Describe feedback you received that was hard to hear.' Same muscle: receive, reflect, change. The structure for both: S-[what happened, no spin], T-[what you were responsible for], A-[how you owned it: who you told, what you fixed, what you changed], R-[the process change and evidence it stuck]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 7. S: '[A real mistake: what broke or went wrong because of your action.]' T: '[Why it was yours to own.]' A: '[Who you told and when, the immediate fix, the process change you made so it cannot recur.]' R: '[Evidence the change worked: the next similar situation went cleanly.]' The R-beat is what separates a confession from a growth story — without the process change, you are just describing a failure; with it, you are describing a professional. Common mistake: the humblebrag — 'my mistake was caring too much.' Panels have heard it a thousand times; it signals you are hiding. A second classic: blaming the tool, the process, or the coworker before owning your part. You may mention contributing factors AFTER owning your part — 'the runbook was unclear, and I should have verified instead of assuming' — but ownership comes first, always. The meta-rule: the panel is not evaluating your mistake; it is evaluating what kind of colleague you are when things go wrong. Be the colleague who raises their hand first. A third integrity prompt - Prompt 8b: 'Tell me about a time you received critical feedback on your technical work.' Distinct from Prompt 8 (hard to hear, personal): this one is about the work product - a code review, a config, an analysis that was wrong. Scaffold: S-[the real feedback: what was wrong], T-[what you were responsible for], A-[how you received it (no defensiveness), verified the critique, fixed the work, changed your review process], R-[the improved output and the process change that stuck]. The scoring: defensiveness is the failure mode. 'My first reaction was to explain why I was right; then I tested their claim, they were right, and I fixed it' is a perfect answer - it shows the honest internal reaction AND the professional override. Panels know everyone feels defensive; they are checking whether professionalism wins. A rehearsal note: this story must be about the WORK, not the person - keep every sentence on the artifact and the process, never on personalities.
notes.title: Prompts 7-8: the mistake and the hard feedback

notes.body: Growth prompts test trajectory: are you becoming more capable, and can you prove it? Prompt 9: 'How do you learn new technology quickly?' The panel wants your method, not your claim — docs-first or lab-first, how you structure practice, how you validate understanding, and a real example with a deadline. Prompt 10: 'Tell me about a time you had to learn something fast for a project.' The compressed version of Prompt 9 with stakes: the deadline, the method, the delivery. Prompt 11: 'What are you learning right now?' — and for you, the honest answer involves this course and the Oct 13 preparation, which is a strong answer if you frame it as operator depth, not video consumption. Scaffold the method explicitly: S-[the technology and the deadline], T-[what you had to deliver with it], A-[your learning sequence: e.g., docs overview, lab build, break-fix reps, teach-back], R-[what you shipped and how the method has held up since]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 9. S: '[A technology you learned under time pressure.]' T: '[What you needed to do with it and by when.]' A: '[Your actual method: the resources, the lab reps, how you tested yourself.]' R: '[What you delivered, and how you still use that method today.]' The A-beat is the whole answer — a candidate with a real method ('I build the smallest working lab, break it three ways, fix each, then teach it to someone') beats a candidate with a real certificate but no method. Common mistake: answering with a list of technologies instead of a method. 'I learned X, Y, and Z' is a resume; the prompt asked HOW. A second trap: claiming you 'just pick things up.' Nobody does — and the panel knows it. Name the reps: the labs, the docs, the failures, the teach-backs. For Prompt 11 specifically, prepare the IL-29 answer now: 'I am rebuilding my endpoint-security depth for this role — allowlisting operations, ringfencing scenarios, Detect triage — with timed drills and a scored mock panel.' That is specific, role-relevant, and verifiable. A fourth growth prompt - Prompt 11b: 'What is the most useful thing you have learned in the last six months?' The panel tests learning velocity and reflection. Your honest answer draws on this course: the specific operator skill (e.g., Detect triage discipline, ringfencing tradeoff reasoning), why it mattered, and how you learned it (the method from Prompt 9). Scaffold: S-[where you started], T-[what you needed], A-[the learning reps], R-[the capability now, with evidence]. The trap: naming something vague ('I learned a lot about security'). The fix: one specific skill, the method, the proof. Specificity signals real learning; vagueness signals real forgetting. Prepare this answer as the capstone of your growth narrative - it is the story of the last six months told as trajectory, and trajectory is what gets offers.
notes.title: Prompts 9-11: learning fast and the growth trajectory

notes.body: Teamwork prompts test collaboration: communication, handoffs, and conflict handled like an adult. Prompt 12: 'Tell me about a time you worked effectively on a team.' The panel wants YOUR collaboration mechanics — how you communicated, how handoffs worked, what you owned inside the team effort. Prompt 13: 'Describe a disagreement with a coworker and how you resolved it.' No villains: the disagreement stated fairly, your approach (listen, data, compromise or escalate properly), the resolution. Prompt 14: 'Tell me about a time you helped a colleague.' Generosity with a real example — what you taught or unblocked, and the outcome. Prompt 15: 'Why ThreatLocker, and why this role?' The closing prompt — connect your trajectory to their mission honestly: zero-trust operations, the Cyber Hero service dimension, and what you bring on day one. Scaffold teamwork stories with the collaboration beats: S-[the real team situation], T-[your specific part], A-[your communication, handoffs, and any friction you navigated], R-[the team outcome plus your measurable contribution]. Worked example — scaffolding Prompt 13. S: '[A real professional disagreement.]' T: '[What was at stake and your role.]' A: '[How you engaged: listened first, brought data, proposed options, accepted the decision or escalated properly.]' R: '[The resolution and the working relationship afterward.]' The R-beat must include the relationship afterward — panels know that unresolved conflict poisons teams, and they are checking that you repair. Common mistake: the conflict story where the other person was simply wrong and you heroically corrected them. That is not conflict resolution; that is a victory lap, and it reads as someone difficult to work with. Show the legitimate other perspective, then your path through it. For Prompt 15, prepare the honest version now: connect your real path — IT operations, the security depth built in this course, the service orientation — to what the role actually does. Specific beats generic: 'your allowlisting-plus-ringfencing model is the most operator-honest endpoint approach I have studied, and the Cyber Hero side matches how I work' beats 'I love cybersecurity.' A final logistics layer: the 24 hours before. Confirm the route and parking the night before - a lost candidate arrives flustered, and flustered fails STAR. Prepare your bag: ID, printed resume copies, a notebook, water. Eat a real breakfast; low blood sugar destroys 90-second discipline. And set the mental frame on the drive: you are not begging for a job, you are showing a panel how you work - the rehearsal already proved you can do it. That frame shift from supplicant to demonstrator changes posture, voice, and answers. Walk in as the operator you have spent weeks becoming, not the applicant hoping to become one. The work is done. October 13 is the demonstration.

objectives: Deliver any behavioral answer in the STAR structure within 60-90 seconds: Situation, Task, Action, Result.
Build 15 prompt scaffolds with two real stories each — filled ONLY with your real history, never invented.
Apply delivery coaching: specific, quantified, honest, first-person actions.
Answer the integrity prompts (mistake, hard feedback, conflict) with ownership and process change.
Handle the no-direct-experience case with bounded honesty instead of fabrication.
Execute the Oct 13 panel-day checklist: rehearsal, logistics, questions, close.

quiz.explain: Situation (one incident), Task (your mission), Action (your steps, first person), Result (measured outcome). The four beats in order, 60-90 seconds.
quiz.q: What does STAR stand for?

choices: The Situation — set the scene thoroughly
The Action — your steps in first person
The Result — skip it if time is short
quiz.explain: The Action gets the most time because the panel is hiring your judgment: what YOU did, in what order, and why. Never skip the Result — unmeasured stories are opinions.
quiz.q: Which STAR beat deserves the most answer time?

choices: Name it plainly, own it fully, show the process change it produced
Pick a trivial mistake to look good
Say you cannot recall any mistake
quiz.explain: The mistake prompt scores accountability, not the mistake. Plain ownership plus a real process change is the passing answer; humblebrags and deflection fail.
quiz.q: How do you answer 'tell me about a mistake you made'?

choices: List every technology you have touched
Say you just pick things up naturally
Describe your learning method with a real deadline-driven example
quiz.explain: The prompt asks HOW you learn. Method plus proof ('docs overview, lab build, break-fix reps, teach-back — used to deliver X by Friday') beats any list.
quiz.q: 'How do you learn new technology quickly?' The panel wants:

choices: Give the closest real situation, name what you did and learned, and note the boundary honestly
quiz.explain: Bounded honesty: the closest real story, plainly framed. Fabrication collapses under follow-up questions; honesty earns trust.
quiz.q: You have no direct experience for a behavioral prompt. What do you do?

choices: 'The user was frustrated because their deadline was at risk, so I listened first, then...'
quiz.explain: Lead with empathy for the person's situation, then your de-escalation and resolution steps. Never badmouth the customer — it fails the prompt instantly.
quiz.q: Which opening passes the difficult-customer prompt?

choices: Name your assumption explicitly and choose the reversible option first
Wait until all information is available
Delegate the decision upward without analysis
quiz.explain: Under uncertainty: state what you know, name the key assumption, prefer reversible moves, update when facts arrive. Panels score the framework, not just the outcome.
quiz.q: A quick decision with incomplete information: the winning approach is:

choices: The other person was simply wrong and you corrected them
A victory lap about winning the argument
The disagreement stated fairly, your approach, the resolution, and the relationship afterward
quiz.explain: Conflict answers need no villains: fair framing, your adult approach (listen, data, options), the resolution, and proof the working relationship survived.
quiz.q: How do you structure the disagreement-with-a-coworker answer?

choices: Ask 2-3 genuine questions about the role, the team, and first-90-days success metrics
quiz.explain: Thoughtful questions signal serious interest and gather real intelligence. 'Nothing' signals disengagement; salary-first signals wrong priorities.
quiz.q: The panel asks 'what questions do you have for us?' Your move:

choices: Review the full question bank once more
Review the panel-day checklist only and trust the rehearsal
Skip breakfast to arrive two hours early
quiz.explain: Game day is performance, not study. New material on the morning creates doubt; the checklist plus rehearsal creates confidence.
quiz.q: Morning of October 13: what do you do?
